transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-03
Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jared Kline (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marco V. (Redwood), Elena Gomez (Mosaic Head of Platform), Marcus Liu (Mosaic SRE), Doris Tan (Mosaic Sec/Comp), Tom Reynolds (Product)

Auto-summary (auto):
- Mosaic is evaluating Redwood for a multi-region serving strategy with strict rollback windows and a "safety-net" fallback for retail peak periods.
- Primary constraints: strict PCI-like data residency for EU customers, on-prem pilot for peak season, SLOs: 99.95% availability and p99 latency targets for checkout-critical flows.
- Next steps: run baseline latency + failover tests, share security docs, draft pilot SOW.

Topics: routing fallback policy, multi-region steering, dedicated vs hosted fit, rollback/rollback window, canary traffic split, network requirements (VPC/KMS), audit logs.

Action items (auto): see metadata action_items.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jared (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro round, then we'll jump into the reliability constraints you mentioned in the intake form.
[00:12] Elena: Thanks, Jared. Yep, happy to be here. Marcus will walk through our current infra.
[00:18] Marcus: Hey, hi, uh Marcus Liu. We run a mixed fleet — GCP in us-central and eu-west for EU customers. We have a small on-prem stack in our Dublin data center for some regulated PII.
[00:30] Priya (SE): Got it. Quick clarifying q — when you say "on-prem" is that for inference or for data residency only?
[00:36] Elena: Mostly for data at rest and the checkout call path — we want the tokens not to cross the public cloud for EU checkout traffic.
[00:44] Tom: Also want a safety-net. During Black Friday we spilled traffic and need a predictable fallback if a region gets noisy.
[00:50] Jared: Perfect. So the safety-net is what we call an automated rollback + model variant fallback plus regional quarantine. We'll unpack that.
[00:58] Priya: Quick note — our platform supports three deployment modes with the same API: Hosted, Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (VPC/on-prem). In practice the tradeoffs for Mosaic will be latency predictability and data path control.
[01:10] Marcus: Right. The p99 checkout path is tough — we need sub 120ms p99 for token-gen calls for the cart recommendation micro-call.
[01:18] Marco: (murmur) Are those token gen calls through a sidecar?
[01:21] Marcus: They're internal microservices, yeah. We do a synchronous call during checkout.
[01:24] Jared: Ok, so two angles: 1) keep the hot path local with Private deployment or Dedicated capacity pinned to eu-west, 2) have a graceful fallback to a Redwood-hosted model in a nearby region with routing policy and circuit breaker thresholds.
[01:38] Doris: We need to understand the data flow. If we fallback to hosted, does user PII leave the EU? That's a non-starter for EU checkout.
[01:46] Priya: Understood. For EU-regulated flows, typical pattern is: keep primary in Private (or Dedicated within customer's VPC in eu-west) and use a route policy that never forwards PII-bearing requests out of region. For degraded modes we can route to a redacted call — strip sensitive fields then call the hosted variant for lower-criticality features.
[02:03] Elena: Hmm, stripping fields is possible but we need to validate with legal. Do you have examples?
[02:07] Priya: Yes, we have a field-redaction pattern in our docs — short link shared in the follow-up. It's basically a transform step in the edge router. (note: doc: https://redwood.example/sec/redaction)
[02:20] Marcus: Ok. On failover, what's the expected downtime during a rollover? We need a quantified rollback window.
[02:26] Jared: Typical automated fallback is sub-30s for routing switch, but the SLO curve depends on connection warmup — e.g., cold KV caches can add 100-300ms for the first few requests. Our canary runbook aims to shift 5-10% first and validate.
[02:42] Tom: Can you explain KV cache warmup? We saw this cause p95 spikes last season.
[02:47] Priya: Sure. For transformer-based models we keep the key-value cache for generation state. When you switch model instances or regions, the cache isn't pre-populated, so first few chat continuations require more compute. We have prefix-caching and priming to mitigate. For Mosaic we recommend prefix priming for checkout templates.
[03:04] Marcus: Do you support cross-region KV replication?
[03:07] Priya: Not full KV replication for live caches, because of consistency and latency tradeoffs. We do snapshot-based priming and progressive warmup — you can also maintain a small hot standby in another region with warmed caches. That's the hot-standby pattern.
[03:19] Elena: What's the cost delta for hot-standby?
[03:22] Marco: (soft) It's roughly 1.5x of single-region if you're keeping GPUs warm; depends on utilization and your model quantization.
[03:29] Marcus: For SLOs we need to define a graceful degradation matrix. Example: checkout-critical -> 99.95% availability, autocomplete -> 99.0%. How does Redwood support multiple SLO tiers?
[03:41] Jared: We let you attach routes to classes: hot path (p99 target 120ms) pinned to Private or Dedicated; warm path (slightly higher latency) to dedicated-hosted hybrids; cold path to hosted with lower SLA. Console allows per-route SLOs and automated fallback policies on breach.
[03:55] Doris: Audit logs — we need request-level audit logs for regulatory review. Are those available in Private?
[03:59] Priya: Yes. Private + Dedicated both support request-level audit logs and can ship to your SIEM or GCS/S3. Hosted can provide aggregated logs and a subset of request metadata, but not full payload for PII flows.
[04:12] Marcus: We're worried about a split-brain scenario during a regional partition — how do you prevent duplicated billing and double-post events?
[04:19] Jared: Good point. For stateful checkout we recommend a single region as source-of-truth. For inference we recommend idempotency tokens on the client and a routing quota that prevents simultaneous dual-post. The routing layer can hold a lease and reject cross-region simultaneous processing. It isn't magic — you need app-level idempotency too.
[04:39] Tom: Ok. On rollback windows — we need an SLA carve-out in our contract: automatic rollback after X failed requests or error rates exceed threshold for Y minutes. Can Redwood automate that?
[04:48] Priya: Yes, Redwood has automated rollback policies in the control plane. You can set a composite condition: error rate > 5% for 3 minutes OR latency breach p99 > 200ms for 2 minutes triggers automatic rollback to previous stable model or region. We can run a canary before full cutover if you want a safer mode.
[05:05] Elena: Who typically owns the rollback? Our on-call or Redwood's on-call?
[05:09] Jared: By default, ops is customer-owned; but our Dedicated enterprise customers often opt for managed fallbacks where Redwood ops can execute a rollback under an agreed runbook and paging matrix. That is part of the Dedicated/Private enterprise support add-on.
[05:21] Doris: For auditing, we need to capture the exact decision chain — what triggered the rollback, who approved, timestamps. Is that stored?
[05:27] Priya: Yes — the control plane records events, alerts, and action history. For Private we can set retention policies and forward to your SIEM.
[05:34] Marcus: On the technical deep-dive side, we want to simulate network partitions. Can Redwood run chaos tests or provide a harness?
[05:41] Jared: We can help coordinate a chaos-run with our SE team. Usually a 2-hr session where we run simulated region flaps and measure end-to-end behavior. We'll need your test harness and a read/write sandbox.
[05:52] Marcus: Good. For the pilot, we want to exercise: (a) failover to hot-standby with warm caches, (b) rollback automation on canary fail, (c) redacted-hosted fallback for non-PII flows. Estimated scope?
[06:03] Priya: That maps well to a 4-week pilot: week 0 onboarding & network setup, week 1 baseline latency tests, week 2 failover/chaos simulations, week 3 runbook finalization & SLO tuning.
[06:13] Elena: Budget question — what's the cost delta for a dedicated hot-standby vs hosted-only fallback?
[06:18] Marco: Very approximate, but for 2-region hot-standby you'd look at roughly 1.4–1.8x of a single-region Dedicated depending on traffic and model size. Hosted-only fallback is cheaper but may not meet data residency constraints.
[06:31] Tom: Any legal or procurement blockers we should know?
[06:34] Doris: We'll need standard DPA + addendum for EU data handling, plus explicit support for customer-managed KMS in Private deployment.
[06:42] Priya: We support customer KMS/HSM integrations in Private and Dedicated; hosted has managed keys with options for bring-your-own-key if you go through our enterprise onboarding. We'll include the KMS integration guide in the follow-up.
[06:54] Marcus: Concerning warmup, can you pre-warm simple prefix templates for the checkout prompts? How long does it stay warm?
[06:59] Priya: Yes. Prefix priming can persist in a warmed cache as long as the instance is kept warm. If you allow instance autoscaling to downscale to zero, you'll lose the cache. So the pattern is a small pinned pool for hot path.
[07:12] Elena: About canary traffic split — we want a conservative approach: 2% initial, ramp to 10% over 10 minutes, validate business metrics. Can Redwood support metric gates beyond just latency/errors?
[07:22] Jared: Absolutely. Our rollout engine supports custom metric gates — you can plug in business metrics from your telemetry (via Datadog/Prometheus) and require those to be green before ramping.
[07:32] Tom: Questions about observability: token-level cost tracing for these routes? We need to understand unit economics during failover.
[07:38] Priya: Console provides per-route token/cost breakdowns and a sim tool to approximate cost for traffic splits. We'll share a sample cost model.
[07:47] Marcus: Security: does failover produce different signatures on requests that would break downstream verification?
[07:52] Priya: We can maintain signing headers through the edge router. If you need payload-level signatures, that needs coordination but it's doable.
[07:59] Doris: A hypothetical: if an EU region flaps and we route to a redacted hosted fallback, we still must retain an audit trail indicating what fields were redacted and why. Can that be stored?
[08:08] Priya: Yes, we can log a redaction fingerprint and rationale without storing PII; that's standard for Private. Hosted has more limitations on payload retention.
[08:17] Elena: We're also exploring a phased model: start with hosted for non-critical routes and move to Dedicated for checkout during peak season. Does Redwood support hybrid routing?
[08:25] Jared: Yes, that's a common path. You can define route priorities: local Dedicated -> private -> hosted-redacted. Policies are composable.
[08:33] Tom: Are there any known failure modes we should plan for that you see a lot?
[08:38] Priya: A few common ones: cache cold start after failover, misconfigured idempotency causing double actions, and insufficient network egress rules blocking VPC callbacks. Also SLO definitions that conflate application latency vs inference latency causing false positives.
[08:51] Marcus: Will Redwood help us tune our SLO thresholds during the pilot?
[08:55] Priya: Yes — we normally run a tuning session post-baseline where we propose p50/p95/p99 thresholds and suggested rollback triggers.
[09:03] Elena: Ok, let's recap so everyone is aligned.
[09:06] Jared: Recap: Mosaic pilot scope — four-week pilot: network & VPC setup, baseline latency + cost modeling, hot-standby failover tests (warm caches), chaos partition testing, and runbook + SLO tuning. Deliverables include an SOW, security docs, test runbook, and a sample routing policy YAML.
[09:22] Tom: Next steps from Mosaic: provide traffic profiles, compliance boundaries, and test harness access.
[09:27] Jared: Redwood next steps: share SOW draft, SOC2/ISO packages, KMS integration guide, and schedule the baseline run.
[09:34] Elena: Sounds good. Any other questions?
[09:36] Doris: Quick one — do you have reference customers who ran a similar hybrid?
[09:40] Marco: We do. We'll anonymize references and share two case studies: one retail, one fintech.
[09:46] Marcus: Great. Thanks everyone.
[09:49] Jared: Thank you. We'll follow up with the materials and calendar invites.

(Transcript notes: occasional ASR errors — e.g., "K-V cash" instead of "KV cache", and speaker attribution may shift mid-sentence.)
